evidence.claim: Rock, woods and rolling country along the St. Croix valley
evidence.quote: Long vistas and rolling landscape in the south changes to a more rugged environment of rock, cliffs and woods as you proceed north.

evidence.claim: The St. Croix Scenic Byway stretches 124 miles between a point north of Sandstone and Point Douglas, near Hastings.
evidence.quote: The 124-mile St. Croix Scenic Byway runs from Point Douglas (near Hastings) to a point north of Sandstone, MN.

evidence.claim: Explore Minnesota presents the drive as a journey through the St. Croix Wild and Scenic River Valley, with rock, cliffs and woods in the north giving way to rolling ground and long views in the south.
evidence.quote: Prepare to be impressed by the great beauty of the St. Croix "Wild and Scenic" River Valley. Long vistas and rolling landscape in the south changes to a more rugged environment of rock, cliffs and woods as you proceed north.

evidence.claim: An earlier route through this country was the Point Douglas to Superior Military Road, begun by the federal government in the 1850s for troop movement.
evidence.quote: In the 1850s the federal government began building the Point Douglas to Superior Military Road.  Although intended as a highway for troop movement

evidence.claim: Civilian and commercial traffic followed, but Minnesota inherited the unfinished road at statehood in 1858 without the money to complete it.
evidence.quote: attracted a flood of civilian and commercial traffic.  When Minnesota achieved statehood in 1858, responsibility for the road devolved to the state, which did not have the funds to finish the project.

evidence.claim: A surviving 1.2-mile section became part of the trail system at Wild River State Park.
evidence.quote: A 1.2-mile (1.9 km) segment was still in evidence when Wild River State Park was established and was incorporated into the park's trail system.

evidence.claim: Rough and unfinished as it was, the military road remained the best route north until railroads arrived in 1870.
evidence.quote: Although very rough and in places incomplete, the road was still the best route north until railroads were built in 1870.

evidence.claim: At Interstate Park, later highway construction took a different form: U.S. Route 8 descends through a rock cut blasted in 1931.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 8 descends through the Minnesota park in a road cut blasted in 1931.

evidence.claim: Traveling south, begin with Sandstone on the Kettle River and Hinckley on the Grindstone River.
evidence.quote: Sandstone is a city in Pine County, Minnesota, United States, along the Kettle River.

evidence.claim: Traveling south, begin with Sandstone on the Kettle River and Hinckley on the Grindstone River.
evidence.quote: Hinckley is along the Grindstone River.

evidence.claim: At Taylors Falls, Interstate Park straddles the basalt gorge of the St. Croix.
evidence.quote: They straddle the Dalles of the St. Croix River, a deep basalt gorge

evidence.claim: At Taylors Falls, Interstate Park straddles the basalt gorge of the St. Croix.
evidence.quote: The towns of Taylors Falls, Minnesota and St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin are adjacent to the park.

evidence.claim: Continue through Stillwater on the river’s west bank to Point Douglas, where the St. Croix meets the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: on the west bank of the St. Croix River

evidence.claim: Continue through Stillwater on the river’s west bank to Point Douglas, where the St. Croix meets the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: located at the convergence of the St. Croix River and the Mississippi River.

evidence.claim: Hinckley’s fire museum occupies a replacement: the railroad depot was rebuilt just after the 1894 fire on the same spot, as an exact replica of its predecessor.
evidence.quote: The museum is located in a restored railroad depot downtown, an exact replica of the pre-fire depot, built just after the fire on the exact same spot.

evidence.claim: The first railroad reached Hinckley in 1869, beginning an expansion of logging and rail traffic.
evidence.quote: The first railroad arrived in Hinckley in 1869; and so began a logging and railroad expansion.

evidence.claim: On September 1, 1894, a firestorm destroyed Hinckley and other northeastern Minnesota towns, killing more than 400 people in and near the town.
evidence.quote: On September 1, 1894, everything changed with a firestorm wiping out Hinckley and many northeastern Minnesota towns, killing over 400 people in the immediate and surrounding areas of town.

evidence.claim: Agriculture then became central to recovery, with potatoes, fruits and vegetables among the crops.
evidence.quote: Hinckley's recovery would hinge on agriculture. Some of the main crops were potatoes, fruits and vegetables.

evidence.claim: The museum tells the story of the fire and the recovery.
evidence.quote: tells the devastating story of what came to be called the Great Hinckley Fire and the town's recovery from it.

evidence.claim: Glacial potholes puncture the basalt at the Dalles of the St. Croix, where two state parks face each other across the river.
evidence.quote: Interstate Park comprises two adjacent state parks on the Minnesota–Wisconsin border, both named Interstate State Park. They straddle the Dalles of the St. Croix River, a deep basalt gorge with glacial potholes and other rock formations.

evidence.claim: Sand and gravel swirling in powerful eddies drilled into the rock; larger stones polished the shafts.
evidence.quote: Within the eddies, the sand and gravel were swirled around with such force that they drilled holes straight down into the rock. Larger rocks caught in the spin would polish the shafts smooth.

evidence.claim: The narrow gorge and sharp turn at Angle Rock later caused repeated logjams during the lumber era.
evidence.quote: The narrow gorge and the sharp turn at Angle Rock caused severe logjams in 1865, 1877, 1883, and 1886.

evidence.claim: Road builders also worked through the basalt: U.S. Route 8 descends through a cut blasted in 1931, followed by stone overlooks and guardrails in the mid-1930s.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 8 descends through the Minnesota park in a road cut blasted in 1931. The Minnesota Department of Transportation built stone overlooks and guardrails along the highway in the mid-1930s.

evidence.claim: The logjams themselves became visitor attractions, drawing as many as a thousand tourists a day.
evidence.quote: The catastrophic logjams drew tourists in droves, as many as a thousand a day.

evidence.claim: Glacial potholes mark the basalt beside the St. Croix gorge.
evidence.quote: a deep basalt gorge with glacial potholes and other rock formations.

evidence.claim: Stillwater takes its name from the calm river near the town center, a name proposed in 1843 by first-sawmill builder John McKusick.
evidence.quote: The name "Stillwater" was proposed in 1843 by John McKusick, who built the settlement's first sawmill.

evidence.claim: Stillwater takes its name from the calm river near the town center, a name proposed in 1843 by first-sawmill builder John McKusick.
evidence.quote: The name derives from the St. Croix River's calmness near the town center.

evidence.claim: Rafts of logs came down the St. Croix, gathered at the boom site upstream and passed through the town’s sawmills.
evidence.quote: For many years, lumbermen sent large rafts of logs down the St. Croix. They were collected at the St. Croix Boom Site two miles upstream of Stillwater, and processed in Stillwater's many sawmills.

evidence.claim: In 1848, a territorial convention at Myrtle and Main streets began the process toward Minnesota statehood.
evidence.quote: In 1848, a territorial convention that began the process of establishing Minnesota as a state was held in Stillwater, at the corner of Myrtle and Main streets.

evidence.claim: Minnesota became a separate territory the following year and a state in 1858.
evidence.quote: Minnesota officially became a separate territory in 1849 and, after population increases, a state in 1858.

evidence.claim: The lift bridge across the St. Croix was completed in 1931, with Minnesota and Wisconsin sharing its construction cost equally.
evidence.quote: In 1931, construction of the Stillwater lift bridge over the St. Croix River was completed at a final cost of $460,174, which was split equally between Minnesota and Wisconsin.
